title: Flat Feet in Adults: When Does It Matter, and Do You Need Surgery?
metaDescription: Most adult flat feet need no treatment. If your arch is dropping with inner-ankle pain: what helps, when surgery is considered and what recovery involves.
intro: Many adults are told at some point that they have flat feet, and many worry that it means trouble ahead. Usually it does not. A flat foot you have always had, that does not hurt, generally needs nothing at all. The flat foot worth paying attention to is a different one: an arch that is gradually dropping in adult life, often on one side, with pain along the inside of the ankle.

sections.heading: Do flat feet in adults need treatment?
sections.body: Usually not. Flat feet are common, and the NHS describes them as usually nothing to worry about: if they are not causing problems, you do not need to do anything. Treatment is for symptoms, not for the shape of the foot. A flexible flat foot that has been the same since childhood and does not hurt is not a reason for insoles, exercises or surgery. What changes the picture is pain, stiffness, weakness, frequent ankle injuries, or a foot that has started to flatten when it was not flat before.

sections.heading: What is a 'collapsing' flat foot, and who gets it?
sections.body: A flat foot that develops in adulthood is most often caused by a failing tibialis posterior tendon, which runs behind the inner ankle bone and holds up the arch. AAOS now calls this progressive collapsing foot deformity. As the tendon is strained, stretched or torn, the arch drops and the heel tilts outward. It is a progressive condition, which is why it is worth assessing early rather than waiting. AAOS notes it is more common in women and people over 40, with obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure as risk factors. Overuse, high-impact sport, a previous injury and non-supportive footwear such as sandals also contribute.
bullets: Pain and sometimes swelling along the inside of the ankle or the arch, often before the foot visibly changes
Pain that is worse after standing for long periods, walking or climbing stairs
Difficulty rising onto tiptoe on the affected foot
Later, pain on the outer side of the ankle as the heel shifts outward and presses against the bone there

sections.heading: How is it diagnosed?
sections.body: Diagnosis starts with examining you standing up, because the arch only shows its true shape under body weight. Two simple tests are especially telling: whether you can rise onto tiptoe on one leg, and whether more toes than usual are visible from behind because the heel has angled outward. Weight-bearing X-rays show alignment and any arthritis. An MRI is used mainly when the diagnosis is uncertain or a tendon tear needs to be confirmed, so it is not routinely needed for every painful flat foot. A CT scan is sometimes used to plan surgery.

sections.heading: What helps without surgery?
sections.body: Most people improve without an operation, according to AAOS, though it takes patience: pain can last more than three months even with early treatment, and longer if it has been present for many months. The aim is to rest and support the tendon while it settles, then strengthen it. None of these measures changes the shape of your foot, but they can relieve pain and may stop it getting worse.
bullets: Supportive, low-heeled shoes in place of flat sandals or chappals for long periods on your feet
Arch-support insoles: off-the-shelf for mild cases, custom orthotics for more marked flattening
An ankle brace, from a simple lace-up type to a more rigid custom brace for stiffer feet
Physiotherapy to strengthen the tendon and stretch a tight calf and Achilles
Lower-impact exercise, and weight loss if you are carrying extra weight
A short period in a boot or cast if the tendon is very inflamed and other measures have failed

sections.heading: Should I have a steroid injection?
sections.body: Generally not into this tendon. AAOS states that steroid injection into the tibialis posterior tendon is not normally done because it can lead to rupture, and the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital lists tendon rupture among the side effects of injection. That matters because a ruptured tendon usually means a larger operation. If pain relief is needed, simple anti-inflammatory tablets, if you can take them safely, together with support and physiotherapy, are the usual route.

sections.heading: When is flat foot surgery actually needed?
sections.body: Surgery is considered when pain persists after several months of proper non-surgical treatment, or when walking has become very difficult. It is not offered to change how a painless foot looks. The operation depends on how flexible the foot is and whether arthritis has set in, and it is often a combination of procedures rather than a single one. A flexible foot can often be corrected while preserving its joints; a stiff or arthritic foot usually needs some joints fused.

table.caption: How the type of flat foot usually shapes the surgical options. A general guide based on AAOS patient information; the actual plan depends on your examination and X-rays.
rows: Early disease, inflamed tendon, little deformity
Cleaning out the inflamed tendon lining, sometimes calf lengthening
Relieve pain and protect the tendon
Flexible flat foot with a failing tendon
Tendon transfer combined with a heel bone realignment (osteotomy) and often ligament repair
Restore support while keeping the joints moving
Fusion of the affected foot joints
Ligament repair, or ankle fusion or replacement
Address the ankle along with the foot

sections.heading: What does recovery from flat foot surgery involve?
sections.body: Recovery is long, and it is worth knowing that before deciding. The Royal Orthopaedic Hospital notes that surgery can be quite extensive and often involves around three months in a cast, and you must keep weight off the foot until your surgeon says it is safe. AAOS advises that it takes six months or more for healing to be complete and pain to improve substantially. Possible complications include pain that is not fully relieved, bones that do not heal together after an osteotomy or fusion, and wound infection; the risk is higher in people with diabetes and in smokers. The more advanced the deformity, the longer the recovery and the less likely a return to high-impact sport.

sections.heading: When should I get my flat foot checked?
sections.body: Get it assessed if your feet are painful, stiff, weak or numb, if you keep injuring your ankle, if walking or balance has become difficult, if you did not have flat feet before, or if only one foot is affected. If you have diabetes and reduced feeling in your feet, any new change in foot shape, or new swelling, warmth or redness, should be seen promptly rather than watched.

faqs.q: Do flat feet in adults need treatment?
faqs.a: Usually not. A flat foot that has always been that way and does not hurt needs no treatment. Assessment is worthwhile if your feet are painful, stiff or weak, if the arch has started to drop in adult life, or if only one foot is affected.

faqs.q: Can flat feet be corrected without surgery?
faqs.a: The shape of an established flat foot does not change with insoles or exercises, but most people with a painful flat foot improve without surgery. Supportive shoes, arch supports or a brace, physiotherapy to strengthen the tendon and calf stretching are the main treatments. Improvement can take more than three months.

faqs.q: Why is my flat foot painful on the inside of the ankle?
faqs.a: Pain along the inner ankle and arch in an adult whose arch is dropping often comes from strain or tearing of the tibialis posterior tendon, which supports the arch. It is a progressive condition, so it is worth having it assessed early.

faqs.q: Is a steroid injection good for flat foot pain?
faqs.a: Steroid injection into the tibialis posterior tendon is generally avoided because it can cause the tendon to rupture. Support, physiotherapy and, where safe, anti-inflammatory tablets are the usual approach.

faqs.q: How long is recovery after flat foot surgery?
faqs.a: It is a long recovery. A period of around three months in a cast is common, with no weight on the foot until your surgeon allows it, and healing typically takes six months or more before pain improves substantially. More severe deformities take longer.
